items.title: England braced for All Black-lash in the ultimate test of their mini-upturn
items.summary:
New Zealand should provide a huge reaction to their shock defeat in Wales with enticing clash even more instructive

From the Bay of Islands on the northern tip of New Zealand to Invercargill in the deep south, there is rare unanimity this week. Back in the day there would be parochial arguments about, say, the ratio of Aucklanders to Cantabrians in the starting XV. This time there is nationwide recognition that absolutely nothing matters beyond a bounce-back win for the boys in black on Saturday.

It is the inevitable upshot of last weekend’s seismic defeat by Wales, a result that prompted Dave Rennie, the head coach, to admit his reshuffled team had “let ourselves and our country down”. The former All Black scrum-half Justin Marshall went a step further. “We were arrogant enough to think that we could make those changes and still protect our history, and now look what’s happened,” a wounded Marshall told the GBRNRZ podcast.

items.title: Gonzalo García: ‘I love Craven Cottage – the fans can reach out and touch you’
items.summary:
Spain Under-21 striker admits the pace of the Premier League has surprised him but says he must stay calm over goal drought at Fulham

The first thing Rita Hayworth’s great nephew says when he walks in is: “Sorry I’m late.” Gonzalo García is not late, but it’s very like him: he is impeccably polite, accommodating, and there’s an almost gentle quality to him, a calm that’s not common but can help, especially in moments when the pressure builds. There’s a reason one of the coaches standing in the rain by the pitch where Spain’s under‑21s have just finished training says everyone here loves García. The Fulham striker shakes hands, introduces himself and ducks into the dressing room to change; then a few minutes later he’s back, apologising for a wait that wasn’t one.

Time to talk, so let’s start with Tinseltown, the family tale. García laughs. His great-aunt, born Margarita Carmen Cansino, was among the biggest stars in Hollywood, although he’s not sure he’s seen any of her films. His grandfather was a surgeon and others in the family followed. His uncles played rugby for Spain, but that wasn’t his thing. As for him, he enrolled in a degree in business management and analytics, and reckons he might have liked law, yet even that wasn’t his chosen field.

Continue reading...
items.t: Gonzalo García: ‘I love Craven Cottage – the fans can reach out and touch you’

items.title: Inside women’s football’s difficult rise in Syria: ‘A joy that everyone in the country needed’
items.summary:
A 14-year civil war ravaged the country and ground women’s football to a halt. Today, the first glimmers of hope are beginning to emerge amid difficulty

In December 2024, Syria’s under-18 women’s football team boarded a last-minute bus at midnight from Aqaba, bound for Damascus. The players had been in Jordan preparing for their final match of the WAFF women’s championship, where a win against Saudi Arabia would have kept their hopes of winning the title alive. Syria pulled out amid fears that the border would close.

Back home, a war that had been largely frozen for four years was suddenly moving at pace. Rebel forces had swept out of the northwest, taking Aleppo and were pushing south towards the capital, 350km away, threatening to topple the now-former president, Bashar al-Assad. Players from the provinces around Damascus made their way home. But those from Hasakah, in the country’s far north-east, spent the next three days stranded at Damascus airport, as airline staff fled and planes sat idle on the tarmac, until a bus was finally able to take them home.

Continue reading...
items.t: Inside women’s football’s difficult rise in Syria: ‘A joy that everyone in the country needed’

items.title: From training clips to thirst traps: why athletes are turning to OnlyFans
items.summary:
A professional sports career does not guarantee wealth. And a growing number of athletes are turning to alternative streams of income

“I’m sick and tired of it.” Bart Swings tossed his jacket behind him. It was August 2025, the Winter Olympics were less than six months away, and the Belgian Olympic champion’s injured knee was not getting better. The clip, profanity and all, later ran on the Belgian evening news along with the weather and the football. But the injury update didn’t come from an interview – it was broadcast on the speed skater’s OnlyFans channel.

The subscription site, best known for porn dudes, cam girls and dubiously horny couples, has quietly assembled one of the stranger rosters in professional sport. The list, about 285 athletes deep, includes Olympic speed skaters and rowers, tennis players, surfers and golfers. And, despite its racy reputation, many of the athletes on OnlyFans are not putting out adult content.

items.t: From training clips to thirst traps: why athletes are turning to OnlyFans

items.title: The unthinkable has come to pass: Tom Brady is a pretty good broadcaster
items.summary:
The former NFL quarterback was widely derided when he started his job in the Fox booth. But he has shown a human side and explains the game beautifully

I have accidentally force-fed myself Tom Brady’s commentary as my primary means of watching the NFL this season. When my favorite team, the Steelers, hired Mike McCarthy as head coach, I lodged a silent protest by declining to spend the several hundred dollars needed to get NFL Sunday Ticket. I didn’t even splurge for RedZone. That means I’ve found myself watching Fox’s NFL broadcasts on a Sunday – often an underwhelming Cowboys game – where Brady is the color commentator in the network’s No 1 booth, alongside play-by-play man Kevin Burkhardt.

This two-and-a-half-month experiment has led me to an alarming conclusion, one I’d seen others reaching gradually over the last year but never taken too seriously myself. Recently, though, the truth has become unavoidable: Tom Brady is pretty good at his job. Gone are the days of the best quarterback of all time being hopelessly outmatched on TV. What has changed is that Brady now sounds like an actual human being.

items.t: The unthinkable has come to pass: Tom Brady is a pretty good broadcaster

items.title: You have to laugh at LIV’s collapse but the saga reveals money is golf’s core value | Jonathan Liew
items.summary:
Why do rich powerful men love golf? Ultimately the sport exists in a world where the politics is assumed to be settled

Farewell, then, LIV Golf. As its original figurehead Greg Norman once so delicately put it, albeit in a slightly different context: we’ve all made mistakes, you learn from those mistakes, and you move forward. Forward – in LIV’s case – to bankruptcy court and the start of liquidation proceedings some time in January 2027. And not without a certain irony, in the sense that Norman’s cherished project, established over a cacophony of human rights concerns, ended up getting dismembered and terminated on the orders of the Saudi government. Life moves on you pretty fast.

Perhaps the funniest part of LIV’s protracted demise – unless you count the television viewing figures – has been the last seven months, after Saudi Arabia abruptly pulled the plug on the seemingly abundant flow of money that had fuelled its astonishing rise. Suddenly LIV’s chief executive, Scott O’Neil, was forced to take his begging bowl up and down midtown Manhattan, panhandling for change, drawing up entirely conceptual revenue forecasts, pretending for all the world that this was an actual, real-life business proposition; a legitimate going concern with profits and a bottom line and a plan for the future.

items.t: You have to laugh at LIV’s collapse but the saga reveals money is golf’s core value | Jonathan Liew

items.title: ‘Closing the door halts growth’: Liv Apps on PWR’s international appeal – and pruning the Red Roses
items.summary:
Saracens and Canada scrum-half believes having fewer overseas players in England’s top tier would be a backwards step both for her and the wider game

Liv Apps understands only too well the benefits of playing in Premiership Women’s Rugby (PWR), so when challenging the views of the Red Roses’ head coach, John Mitchell, it comes from the heart. According to the Saracens and Canada scrum-half, limiting the international talent pool in England’s elite division would halt the growth of the game, or even dilute the PWR’s potency.

“For us Canadians, it is amazing to have the PWR because we don’t have a league at home. But then also what the Canadians and the other internationals bring to the England players, we all make each other better.”
